title: Om tat sat (17.23–17.28)
hook: three short words that begin and bless an action

segments.voice: Yesterday: food, sacrifice, austerity, gift, three kinds each. Your line was which kind. Did you ask it at a meal? Today, three words that close the chapter. Day two hundred eighteen.

Before a runner starts, she touches the line. Before a pianist plays, a breath, hands in the lap. Before a family eats, some pause, some say a word. People mark the start of things that matter. Chapter seventeen has spent a whole day sorting actions into three kinds. Now, at the very end, it offers three words, not for sorting, but for beginning. Om. Tat. Sat. You've already met the first one. It was your second word, back in camp one, the sound before words.
screen: `TOUCH THE LINE.` → `A BREATH BEFORE THE FIRST NOTE.` → `THREE WORDS TO BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-three. Om tat sat: this is remembered as the threefold name of Brahman, the ultimate. By it, long ago, the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order. Then Krishna explains each word. Om first. Verse twenty-four: so those who follow the Veda always begin their acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline by saying om. The sound goes first. Tat means that. Verse twenty-five: with tat, people seeking freedom do their sacrifice, discipline and giving without aiming at the reward. It's a way of saying, this isn't for me; it's for that. And sat means real, true, good. Verse twenty-six: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for any praiseworthy act. Verse twenty-seven: steadiness in sacrifice, discipline and giving is called sat, and so is any action done for its sake. So the three words make a small arc. Om: begin with the sacred sound. Tat: offer it to that, not to yourself. Sat: let it be real and good. And then the chapter's last verse, twenty-eight, is a warning that ties back to faith. Whatever is offered, given or practiced without faith is called asat, unreal. It counts for nothing, here or after. The Sanskrit prefix a means not, so asat is simply not-sat. Some printed editions also set these three words in each chapter's closing line, a way of handing the chapter back. That's the word today: om tat sat.
screen: `THE THREEFOLD NAME.` · `OM: BEGIN WITH THE SOUND.` · `TAT: FOR THAT, NOT FOR ME.` · `SAT: REAL AND GOOD.` · then, large: `OM TAT SAT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one thing you'll do after this. Something ordinary. Cooking, a call, a task at work. Take the first breath as om: the beginning, the sound before words. Take the second as tat: this isn't only for me. Take the third as sat: may it be real and good. If you'd like, you can say the three words softly. Then just sit, and let the action wait. The bell holds the time.
Om tat sat. Gita seventeen, twenty-three: the threefold name of the ultimate. Om, the sacred sound; tat, that; sat, the real and good.
Your line: om tat sat. Before one ordinary task today, pause for three breaths: begin, offer, make it real. Day two hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: Some Hindus say 'om tat sat' at the close of a reading, a ritual or a teaching; some printed Gitas set the three words in each chapter's closing line, and verse 17.24 says Vedic rites begin with om.

myth: om tat sat is called the threefold name of Brahman in Gita 17.23
by it the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order.
sat means only 'existence' and has nothing to do with goodness
verse 26: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for praiseworthy acts.
the Gita says acts done without faith still count fully
verse 28: they're called asat, and count for nothing, here or after.

fork.setup: you're about to begin an act of giving and you want it to be for that, not for you. which word does verse 25 attach to this?
fork.reveal: tat, that. seekers of freedom act with tat, without aiming at the reward.

original.note: Sanskrit: om (the sacred syllable), tat (that), sat (the real, the good); the threefold name in Gita 17.23.

trapdoor: what you thought: om tat sat is a chant with no clear meaning.
what it means: three words that begin an act with the sacred sound, offer it to that, and name it real and good.
what a scholar hears: 17.23 calls it the triple designation (nirdesha) of Brahman; 17.28 names acts without shraddha asat; the phrase recurs in the chapter colophons of some editions.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 17.23 (the threefold name of Brahman)

notes: 'In many editions... these three words appear at the close of every chapter': chapter colophons in many editions include 'om tat sat'; confirm wording for the edition the path uses.
The practice invites saying the three words softly, optional; no new prayer is written.
Editor review (2026-10-01): 'many editions... every chapter' and 'people everywhere' softened; howItsDone's 'many Vedic rites begin with om' now tied to what 17.24 says.
